conversation_lines.text: Yes, being subtherapeutic increases your risk of another clot. We’re starting you on IV heparin to bridge while we adjust your warfarin dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I’m scared of another clot. But I also don’t want to go back to that rehab place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I heard your concerns. You mentioned another patient is wandering and aggressive?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, he’s been yelling, hitting walls, and staff say they can’t control him. I’m in a wheelchair—I can’t protect myself if he comes near me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s not safe. We’ll work with social work to find a different extended care facility for discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your CT scan from yesterday shows the pulmonary embolism has resolved. That’s great news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? So why am I still having chest pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t think it’s your heart or lungs now. Your EKG and troponins are stable. The pain seems more like inflammation in the chest wall—called costochondritis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Costo-what? Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not dangerous. It’s like a muscle or cartilage strain in your chest. It can feel sharp and get worse when you press on it. We’ll start a muscle relaxer called methocarbamol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I can’t take NSAIDs because of my kidneys and allergy, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. So methocarbamol is safer for you. We’ll also keep your heart meds—like metoprolol, atorvastatin, and clopidogrel—to protect your bypass grafts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You just finished dialysis. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Tired, but no chest pain since this morning. That new pill might be helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’re also switching your phosphate binder from sevelamer to lanthanum because you can’t crush sevelamer, and you need your pills crushed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I can’t swallow big pills since my esophageal tear. Is lanthanum safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and it works well for dialysis patients. We’ll start low and adjust based on your labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR was 1.7 yesterday—still low. We’re adjusting your heparin and will check it again today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will I need heparin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Until your INR is in the safe range—around 2 to 3. That could take a few more days. You’ll stay on warfarin for at least three months after the PE.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And then I can stop?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll decide that later. If the clot was unprovoked, you may need longer treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is now 2.1—much better. We’re reducing the heparin and will stop it soon if it stays up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. My chest feels better too. But my feet still hurt at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you have neuropathy from diabetes. We’re keeping gabapentin and doxepin—they help nerve pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They help a little. Can we try something stronger?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We have to be careful with other pain meds because of your kidney disease. Let’s give this combo a bit more time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is 2.5 today—perfect. We’re stopping the heparin infusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great! So I’m just on Coumadin now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll monitor it closely after discharge. You’ll need regular blood tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know. DaVita does that for me. But will the new rehab place be ready?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Social work is arranging it. You’ll go to a different facility—same level of care, but safer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s your chest pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I only had a twinge when I moved wrong. The methocarbamol really helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep it on your discharge list, four times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my Imdur? I can’t swallow big pills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve changed it to a short-acting nitrate you can crush. It’ll still help with any heart-related chest tightness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable. Creatinine is expected for dialysis, and potassium is normal now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had high potassium before. Was that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, very high potassium can affect your heart rhythm. But we caught it early, and dialysis corrected it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge on Friday. You’ll go to the new rehab center for physical therapy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel safer knowing I won’t go back to that place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send all your meds crushed, and the center will continue your dialysis on Tues, Thurs, and Sat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check: chest pain gone, INR stable, dialysis done. You’re doing really well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel stronger. Can I walk more at the new place?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, physical therapy will help with that. You’ve had a stroke before, so building leg strength is important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Discharge papers are ready. You’re leaving tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can you go over my meds again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. You’ll take warfarin daily, methocarbamol four times a day, gabapentin twice a day, and the crushed nitrate as needed. Lanthanum with meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Back to your usual—2 units of Novolog at meals. Check your blood sugar four times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if my chest pain comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use the nitrate. If it doesn’t help, or you have shortness of breath, call your doctor or go to ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And weigh myself daily, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Call if you gain more than 3 pounds in a day—could be fluid buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to leave. The transport team will take you to the new rehab center in an hour.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better and safer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep up with your meds, dialysis, and follow-up. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for listening to me about the rehab place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Your safety is important. Have a smooth recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been having pain in my left breast since they did a biopsy last week. It smells bad and won’t heal. And my right heel has been hurting a lot too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. The breast clinic sent you over because of concern about infection, and your heel pain raised questions about a possible ulcer. We’ve started some antibiotics to cover possible infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh good. I was worried. The dressing wasn’t changed after the biopsy, and I didn’t know what to do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That may have contributed to the infection. We’ll keep the wound clean with regular dressing changes. We also checked your foot with an X-ray, and there’s no fracture or bone infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a diabetic ulcer? My last one was really bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it doesn’t look infected. It’s a healing pressure injury, likely from sitting or lying too long on one side. We’ll make sure you’re offloading pressure from that heel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I haven’t been moving much since my knee surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll work with wound care to help it heal. Now, about your breast wound — we swabbed it, and it showed multiple bacteria, including Pseudomonas, which is sensitive to the antibiotics we’re using.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pseudomonas? Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, especially in someone with your health conditions, but we caught it early. The antibiotics should clear it. We also did an ultrasound of your breast — no abscess, so no need for surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank goodness. I was scared they’d have to cut again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll avoid that if we can. You’ll stay on IV antibiotics for now, then switch to oral later. We also found something in your urine — signs of infection with debris in the bladder.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been going a lot, but only a little comes out. Is that from the infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and because your kidneys don’t make much urine, bacteria can build up. We placed a catheter briefly to clear the sludge — it’s more likely sludge than pus — and we’re treating with strong antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m on dialysis three times a week — does that affect the infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it does. Your immune system is weaker, and antibiotics don’t reach the bladder well. That’s why we’re using IV meds for now. You’ll continue dialysis as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are stable. We checked your blood cultures — no growth, which is great. That means the infection hasn’t spread.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about the swelling in my legs? I’ve had that for days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an ultrasound to check for blood clots. You declined imaging of the right knee area, but we saw no clots in the rest. The swelling is likely from heart and kidney issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t want the probe pressing on my knee — it still hurts. But I’m glad it’s not a clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understood. We’ll monitor it. Your heart function is stable — no signs of worsening failure. We’re keeping an eye on your fluid balance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today, wound care did a gentle debridement of your breast wound — just removing dead tissue to help it heal. It looked better — less odor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It does feel a bit better. Will I need more of that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but only if needed. The main thing is keeping it clean and on antibiotics for two weeks total.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my warfarin? I was on it for a blood clot before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR was 1.0 on admission — you weren’t taking it. Since your prior clot was after surgery, and you’ve had five months of treatment, we’re not restarting it. Your primary doctor agrees.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t trust the rehab — they didn’t change my dressing. I left and came home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We spoke with social work. Your sister and niece will help you at home with care. We’ll arrange home health nursing for wound checks and support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they’ll be with me. I just want to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat leg ultrasound showed no clots. We’ll keep your legs elevated and monitor swelling. How’s your pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. The oxycodone helps, but I don’t want to take too much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve kept your gabapentin dose lower due to kidney function. We’ll continue the lidocaine patch and methocarbamol for muscle pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine culture came back — mixed bacteria, likely contamination. But given your symptoms, we’re confident the treatment is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the catheter helped clear it out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we removed it after one day. No more drainage. We’re switching back to oral ciprofloxacin and clindamycin for the breast infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I take those at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for a total of 14 days. We’ll send them with you. Also, a miconazole powder for the dry rash on your right breast.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Wound care did another debridement this morning. The tissue looks healthier. Your white count is down — that’s a sign the infection is improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can see it’s not as red. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If things keep improving, likely in a few days. We’ll make sure your pain is controlled and your home support is set up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news — your breast wound has no foul odor today. The antibiotics are working. We’ll plan for discharge tomorrow if dialysis goes well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. I’ve missed my family.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve scheduled a breast clinic follow-up in two weeks. They’ll monitor the healing and the small benign-looking lump we saw on ultrasound.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The one at 12 o’clock? Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s BI-RADS 3 — probably benign. They just want to check it in three months with another ultrasound.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Last day in the hospital. Your labs are stable. Dialysis went well. You’re cleared to go home tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. What do I need to watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking all your meds, especially the antibiotics. Check your weight daily — call if you gain more than three pounds in a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the wound? How often should I change the dressing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nursing will visit and do it twice a day. You or your sister can help after they show you. Keep the heel offloaded — no sitting or lying on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my insulin — should I adjust it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No changes — keep your usual doses. Your last A1c was 7.1%, which is good. We’ll keep your other meds the same, with a few small dose adjustments for your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like the gabapentin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, now once every other day. And allopurinol every other day too. The rest are the same. We’ll send a full list with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure my sister sees it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re officially discharged. You’ve done well — infection is clearing, wounds are healing, and you’re stable on all your conditions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel so much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember — finish all antibiotics, keep follow-up appointments, and call if you have fever, increased pain, or swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And thank you for listening to me about going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Your care team worked hard to make that happen safely. Take care, and we’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave. Your vitals are stable — temperature 98.5, blood pressure 123/41. Breathing well, no new issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My heel still hurts, but not as bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. Keep using the walker and offloading the heel. The bone spurs may cause some ongoing discomfort, but the wound is healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing — your sister will help you with the insulin and meds, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, she’s been trained. And the nurse will come twice a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re all set. We’ll call you to check in, and see you in follow-up. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again. I’m so grateful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you came in because your dialysis access wasn't working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I couldn't get dialysis today. My arm felt fine, but they said no blood flow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You also mentioned painful bumps on your abdomen where you inject insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they've been getting bigger for three weeks. I finished antibiotics but no improvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And you've had burning when you urinate and cloudy, smelly urine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for about three weeks. I finished another antibiotic but still feel the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We'll check your arm, abdomen, and urine. You're not running a fever, but we'll start antibiotics just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. I'm worried about my dialysis access failing again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We'll get imaging on your arm tomorrow to see what's going on. For now, rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your CT scan shows your bladder wall is inflamed, likely infection. The abdominal bumps aren't abscesses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it's not calciphylaxis again? I couldn't tolerate that treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No calcium deposits were seen. We'll watch them as possible panniculitis. No treatment change now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That's a relief. What about my arm?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have a clot in your AV graft. You'll have a procedure today to clear it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it work? I've had clots before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The radiologist is experienced. They'll use medication and tools to open it. Success is likely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The procedure was successful. The clot is gone, and blood is flowing through your graft.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you! Can I do dialysis tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, scheduled for tomorrow. We'll also check your breast wound.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It's been oozing a little. Is it infected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We took a sample. It grew E. coli and Proteus, both sensitive to the antibiotic we're giving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like last time? That was painful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Different bacteria, but we're treating it effectively. Ultrasound shows no abscess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. What about my urine infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The culture was contaminated, so we can't confirm. But your symptoms are improving with antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You completed dialysis yesterday. Your labs are improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel better. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We want to finish your IV antibiotics. You'll get them during dialysis sessions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I'll go home and come back for antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the antibiotic will be given after each dialysis. We'll switch to oral if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my wound care?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Wound care team recommends daily dressing changes with saline and special packing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can do that at home with help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and follow up with your wound nurse practitioner.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count is down, creatinine improving. You're healing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any news on the back spot from the CT?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The lytic spot in your spine is likely benign, maybe a Schmorl's node. MRI can clarify if needed later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I'd rather not unless it's urgent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Agreed. We'll monitor. Your blood pressure is stable on your meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're doing well. We'll plan discharge tomorrow if labs stay stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I'm ready to go home. Will I need rehab?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Physical therapy says you can go home with support. We'll arrange services.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final labs look good. Your infection markers are down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You'll get ceftazidime after each dialysis for now. Repeat urine culture if symptoms return.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my abdominal bumps?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Follow up with dermatology if they change. No treatment now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're cleared to go home. Take your meds, do wound care, and attend dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for fixing my access and treating the infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're welcome. Call if you develop fever, chest pain, or trouble breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And check labs in a week?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and follow up with nephrology and your primary team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glad to hear it. You handled everything well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again, doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We'll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I'll make sure to keep all my appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That's the best way to stay healthy. Safe travels home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. Call us with any concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you came in because your dialysis access wasn’t working today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. The nurses at dialysis tried to use my arm graft, but couldn’t get it to work. I’ve had this before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I see you were here about a month ago for the same issue. We’ll need to check your graft again. How are you feeling otherwise?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel okay. No chest pain, no shortness of breath. Just worried I can’t get dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. We’ll make sure you get dialysis while you’re here. First, we’ll do some blood work and get you set up for a procedure tomorrow to look at your graft.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will they try to fix it again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the transplant surgery team will do a fistulogram and try to clear the clot. But sometimes, if it’s blocked too much, we may need a temporary catheter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a catheter once before. I didn’t like it in my neck.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We only use it temporarily. It helps us keep your dialysis on schedule while your arm graft heals or gets repaired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, as long as it’s not forever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You just came back from the procedure. The team tried to open up your graft, but there was a tough blockage they couldn’t fully clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it didn’t work?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not completely. They opened part of it, but there’s still a narrow spot that didn’t respond to the balloon. Because of that, they decided to place a temporary catheter in your neck for dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s very common. We’ll make sure it’s clean and monitored. You’ll get dialysis through it today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my arm? Will they try again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The surgeons recommend an outpatient procedure to repair the graft. They’ll contact you to schedule it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s good to know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable. Your kidney numbers are improving after dialysis. We’ll keep an eye on your blood counts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been anemic before. Is that still a problem?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is lower than ideal, but it’s expected with kidney disease. You’re on erythropoietin, which helps. We’ll keep monitoring it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an ultrasound on your abdominal wound yesterday. Good news — no abscess or fluid collection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s still tender. Should I keep cleaning it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The wound care team recommends cleaning it with a wound cleanser, applying DuoDerm gel, and covering it with a Mepilex dressing every three days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the antibiotics? I was on ceftazidime before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Since there’s no sign of active infection, we’re not continuing IV antibiotics. But you’ll keep the wound care at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my breast wound? It’s still packed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That wound is healing. We’ll keep packing it daily. You should follow up with the breast clinic as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick update — we’ve replaced the temporary catheter in your neck with a tunneled one. It’s more secure and meant for longer use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that the same one?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a better version — same spot, but it goes under the skin and is less likely to get infected or move out of place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news — you’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Already? What about dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go back to your regular dialysis schedule using the catheter in your neck. The transplant team will contact you to fix your arm graft as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my wounds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have a visiting nurse come to help with both wounds. They’ll follow the same cleaning and dressing routine we’ve been doing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad I won’t be alone with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll also send your medications home with you. Most are the same, including your insulin, heart meds, and pain patches.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No more IV antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, we’re stopping those. The wounds aren’t infected now, so we don’t need them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better knowing what’s next.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll make sure your daughter gets a call with the discharge details. You’ll be going home with support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: She’ll be relieved. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I'll be taking care of you during this admission. You're here because your left arm dialysis access isn’t working—it’s clotted again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I couldn’t get dialysis yesterday. My arm felt cold and numb. Is it fixable this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to try. You’ve had this graft for a while, and it’s had multiple clots. The last imaging showed a problem with the artery feeding it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s the plan? Another surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re scheduling you for a procedure tomorrow morning—left arm exploration. We’ll see if we can open the clot and fix the blood flow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if you can’t fix it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll use your tunneled catheter in your neck for dialysis. It’s already in place, so we can use it right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I just want to get back on track with dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get you there. For now, we’ll run some blood tests and monitor your heart, given your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs came back. Your hemoglobin is low, but stable. Kidney numbers are as expected for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been anemic for years. Is that still from my kidneys?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s part of your end-stage renal disease. We’re not giving any transfusions now, but your team will manage it long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. I’ve also been nauseous—can’t keep pills down sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I saw that. You tried the long-acting nitrate and vomited. We’re switching you to a smaller, short-acting one three times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That might help. The big pill always made me sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re going to surgery in an hour. The goal is to fix the graft, but we might find that it can’t be saved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. Just do what’s safest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re back. The surgery didn’t go as hoped. We opened the area, but the artery feeding the graft is too small and already past the split.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So you couldn’t fix it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. The blood flow wouldn’t be strong enough. We decided not to create a new connection. Your graft is no longer usable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’ll be on the neck catheter for good?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, yes. You have a follow-up with your access surgeon to discuss options—maybe a new graft in your right arm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a lot. But as long as I can keep dialysis, I’ll manage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll get you dialyzed today. The catheter was sluggish, so we’ll use TPA to clear it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: TPA? Isn’t that for strokes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same medication, but here we use a small dose inside the catheter to dissolve clots. It’s safe and common.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your dialysis session completed. We couldn’t remove fluid because your blood pressure dropped, but the treatment worked.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt dizzy. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially with your heart history. We’ll adjust your settings at the outpatient unit to go slower.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my chest X-ray—was it okay? I had some shortness of breath after surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the X-ray showed your lungs are clear. No pneumonia or fluid. Your heart is large, but that’s chronic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving you another dose of TPA in the catheter overnight to keep it open. We’ll flush it out tomorrow before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that affect my bleeding risk?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Minimal risk—it’s only in the catheter, not your bloodstream. We’re watching closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We removed the TPA from your catheter. Your incision is healing well—no signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’m going to rehab today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, to the extended care facility for 30 days. You’ll keep going to outpatient dialysis three times a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my other follow-ups?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your gynecologist will contact you about the ultrasound. You have a heart and access clinic follow-up scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember—the ultrasound showed fibroids and something about the lining?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the endometrium was slightly thick. They’ll want to check it more closely, but it’s not urgent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my meds—are they the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mostly. The long-acting nitrate is replaced with a smaller pill three times a day. You can crush it in applesauce if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’ll help. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember—no blood pressure checks or blood draws on your left arm. Keep the incision dry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And no heavy lifting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Nothing over 10 pounds. Call the access clinic if your hand turns blue, cold, or numb.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. The rehab team will help you transition. We’ll keep coordinating with your doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Let’s get your discharge papers ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave—your vitals are stable, and you’re alert and walking well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready. Nervous, but ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. You’ve been through a lot. The rehab team knows your plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And dialysis starts tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, at your usual center. They’re expecting you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ll see them then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Call if anything changes before your follow-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I'll be taking care of you during your stay. You came in with chest pain, nausea, and vomiting after dialysis yesterday. Can you tell me more about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, right after my dialysis session, I started feeling sick—nauseous, then vomiting. And this chest pain came on, like a thumping, going to my left shoulder. I felt dizzy too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any shortness of breath or fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no fever or trouble breathing. Just the chest pain and nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We checked your heart enzymes and EKG. Your troponin was slightly elevated but stable, and the EKG changes look like they might be from lead placement, not a heart attack.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my heart again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It doesn’t look like a new heart attack. We’ll keep monitoring, but we think your symptoms may be from other causes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also noticed two painful areas—one on your inner thigh and one on your left hip. They’re firm and discolored. Have they been getting worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they’ve been sore and hard. I thought it was cellulitis, so I’m on Bactrim.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re concerned it might be calciphylaxis, a condition where calcium builds up in the skin. We’ll do a CT scan and possibly a biopsy to confirm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Calciphylaxis? I’ve heard of that. Isn’t it serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, but we’re catching it early. We’ll start treatment if confirmed. Also, your urine test showed signs of infection—white blood cells and bacteria.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been having some burning when I pee. Could that be it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that fits. Since you have kidney disease, this is a complicated UTI. We’re starting IV antibiotics, then switching to oral cipro.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CT scan is back. It shows calcifications in your blood vessels and in the skin nodules on your thigh. This supports calciphylaxis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s confirmed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not fully. We’ll do a punch biopsy tomorrow to be sure. If positive, we’ll start sodium thiosulfate, which helps remove calcium from tissues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a small biopsy, done with local numbing. You’ll feel a pinch, but it’s quick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did the biopsy this morning. It confirmed calciphylaxis—calcium deposits in the small blood vessels of your skin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. So what now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting sodium thiosulfate during dialysis. You’ll need daily dialysis for a week, then four times a week. This helps clear the calcium.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Daily? That’s a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. But it’s important to stop new lesions. We’ll adjust after your nephrologist sees you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m feeling nauseous again. Is it the new medicine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sodium thiosulfate can cause nausea. We’re also checking if your calcium acetate is contributing. We may switch to lanthanum.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had nausea with calcium acetate before. Maybe that’s it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching you to lanthanum. We’ll also give you Zofran and Ativan for nausea as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure has been high—around 180s over 60s. We’re increasing your isosorbide dinitrate to 30 mg three times a day and starting amlodipine 5 mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on blood pressure meds for years. Why’s it so hard to control?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: With kidney disease, it’s tougher. We’ll keep adjusting. You may need more changes after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My belly wound is still sore. Is it healing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Wound care checked it. They say it’s improving—good pink tissue, no infection. Keep following up with transplant surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are looking better. White count is down, kidney function stable. The antibiotics are working on your UTI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I haven’t had burning when I pee since yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a great sign. You’ll finish a 14-day course of cipro to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The sodium thiosulfate still makes me nauseous, but I can handle it if it helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m proud of you for sticking with it. We’ll keep managing the nausea. Dermatology will see you next week to check the lesions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Pain is controlled, nausea improved, and your wounds are stable. We’re planning discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Where will I go?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: To an extended care facility for rehab and dialysis support. You’ll need help with daily dialysis four times a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue cipro for the UTI, lanthanum instead of calcium acetate, higher-dose blood pressure meds, and oxycodone for pain. Dilaudid for breakthrough pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the sodium thiosulfate?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Three times a week during dialysis. We’ll coordinate with your outpatient team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about managing all this at home later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. The rehab team will help you practice. You’ll have follow-ups with nephrology, dermatology, and transplant surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my chest pain hasn’t come back. That’s good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and your heart tests stayed stable. We think the nausea and UTI triggered the episode.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad it wasn’t my heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do one more set of labs today. If they’re good, you’ll be discharged tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready to go, but I’ll miss the nurses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ve been great. You’ve made real progress—UTI clearing, pain controlled, and on track with calciphylaxis treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are stable. We’re ready to discharge you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What do I need to do next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Finish your cipro, keep up with four-times-weekly dialysis, and take sodium thiosulfate three times a week. Watch for new skin sores.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-ups?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Dermatology in one week, transplant surgery for your wound, and your nephrologist to adjust dialysis and meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep up the good work. Call if you have fever, worsening pain, or new symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave. How’s your pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s manageable. I used Dilaudid once yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Keep the oxycodone regular and Dilaudid as needed. And remember, no aspirin—we use Plavix instead due to your allergy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. No aspirin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure is 187/62—still a bit high. Keep taking the new doses. We’ll follow up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll watch it at the facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they’ll help. And keep the wound clean. No soaking in baths.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done really well. Stay on top of your appointments and meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The transport team will be here soon to take you to the extended care facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send all your records and prescriptions ahead.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll be in touch with your outpatient team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Keep it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See you soon in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Ms. ___. I’m Dr. ___. I understand your dialysis line wasn’t working—can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I went for dialysis four days ago, but they couldn’t use my line. They replaced it this morning, but it still didn’t work when I got back to dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. We’ve reviewed your labs and imaging. There was a fibrin sheath around the old catheter, which likely caused the blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A what sheath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A fibrin sheath—it’s like a thin layer of clot that can form around the catheter and block blood flow. We tried using tPA to dissolve it, but it didn’t work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll place a new catheter tomorrow. The radiology team will do it under imaging guidance to make sure it’s positioned correctly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it work this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re hopeful. We’ll also use a balloon to clear any remaining blockage in the vein. Most patients do well after this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, you mentioned left heel pain—how long has that been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: About four weeks. No injury, just constant ache. It’s worse when I walk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get an X-ray to rule out a fracture. Given your history, it could be plantar fasciitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s inflammation in the tissue along the bottom of your foot. Common in people with diabetes and kidney disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your X-ray showed no fracture, but there’s thickening of the plantar fascia—consistent with plantar fasciitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no break, just inflammation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll manage it with rest, pain meds, and possibly physical therapy later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Now, about your dialysis line—we placed a new one this morning. It’s a split-tip catheter, designed to reduce clotting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And it’s working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the flow is good. You’ll have dialysis later today, and we’ll monitor it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white blood cell count was elevated when you came in—13.4. It’s now down to 8.5, which is better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Was I infected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. The dermatology team looked at your thigh wounds—those from your calciphylaxis—and noticed pus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, those are so painful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They took a deep culture. It grew several bacteria, including Pseudomonas, which can be serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pseudomonas? Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, especially in wounds. But your culture showed it’s sensitive to ciprofloxacin, so we’re treating it with cipro and clindamycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will I need antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Ten days total. You’ve started today, so you’ll finish after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll take them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also got your PTH level from your outside records—it’s very high, 1110.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What does that mean?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means you have severe hyperparathyroidism. That’s likely driving your calciphylaxis—those painful skin lesions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can we fix that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Surgery to remove your parathyroid glands—parathyroidectomy—is the best option. Dermatology recommended it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Surgery? I’m scared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But without it, the calciphylaxis will keep getting worse. You’ll follow up with the surgeon after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll go. But I don’t want those injections they mentioned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You mean the intralesional sodium thiosulfate? That’s okay—you refused, and we respect that. We’ll focus on the surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your wounds are being cared for by the wound team. They’re changing the dressings regularly and packing them properly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They hurt so much when they change them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. We’ll give you pain meds before each change. It’s important to keep the wounds clean to prevent more infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. Your dialysis is working, your infection is responding, and your pain is better controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go to an extended care facility. You’ll continue dialysis there and finish your antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see Dr. ___ next week to discuss parathyroidectomy. That’s the next big step.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to discharge. Your new catheter is working well, and your wounds are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take cipro and clindamycin for ten days, plus your other meds like cinacalcet and sevelamer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to take them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And keep the dressings clean. The facility will help you with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll go to the surgeon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We’ll be following up with your sister to make sure everything goes smoothly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: She’s been so helpful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad. Take care, Ms. ___. We’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your heel pain should improve with rest. Avoid standing too long.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll take it easy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And call if the pain worsens or you develop redness or swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright, the transport team will take you shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you came in today because of worsening pain in your skin wounds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. The pain in my left hip, right breast, and belly got much worse during dialysis. It’s sharp and comes and goes, but it’s worse at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You’ve been dealing with calciphylaxis for a while. The ER team started you on IV antibiotics—clindamycin and cipro—because there’s concern for infection in the wound areas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had that same infection last month. They gave me antibiotics then. Is it back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. The gram stain from your thigh ulcer showed a small amount of bacteria, mostly white blood cells and some gram-positive cocci. It’s not a heavy infection, but we’re treating it to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. But the pain is mostly from the calciphylaxis, not just infection, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The calciphylaxis is the main issue—those chalky, firm areas on your skin are calcium deposits. They’re very painful. Dermatology recommends trying intralesional sodium thiosulfate injections once you’re out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I couldn’t tolerate the IV version before—made me vomit. Are the shots better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, these are injections directly into the wounds. They’re usually better tolerated and can help heal the lesions and reduce pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m willing to try. Anything to stop this pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs this morning show your white count is coming down—from 12.6 to 10.9—so the antibiotics are helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Is my kidney function okay? I’m worried about that too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine is up a bit to 4.3, but that’s expected. You’re still on dialysis three times a week. The nephrology team increased your cinacalcet to 60 mg twice daily to help control your PTH and slow the calciphylaxis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember they said I might need surgery on my parathyroid glands. Is that still the plan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Outpatient surgery is still recommended. We’ll follow up with the surgeon once you’re stable. For now, we’re focusing on infection control and pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re getting ready to discharge you to the extended care facility. You’ll finish a 7-day course of oral clindamycin and ciprofloxacin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I need to follow up with dermatology for the injections?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We couldn’t schedule it yet, but if you don’t hear from them in two business days, call the clinic directly. Also, keep taking your oxycodone as needed for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I really want to switch dialysis centers. The one I’m at isn’t good to me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’ve noted that. The care team will help you explore other options. Your health and comfort matter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel a bit better. The pain isn’t gone, but it’s more manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good progress. Keep up with wound care, take your meds, and follow up with your doctors. You’re doing the right things.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure I do. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you had some vomiting with blood after dialysis tonight. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I got really nauseous like I usually do after dialysis, but this time I saw coffee-ground stuff in the vomit. I’ve never seen that before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. That’s concerning. We’ve placed a small tube through your nose to check your stomach. It showed only a little coffee-ground material, no active bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it serious? I’ve thrown up after dialysis for years, but never with blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be a small tear from vomiting, which often heals on its own. Your blood count is stable, so we don’t think you’re actively bleeding. We’ll keep you NPO for now and give you medication to reduce stomach acid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. But I’ve been so nauseous lately—could it be from my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s possible. We’re reviewing your medications. Sodium thiosulfate, which you take for calciphylaxis, can cause nausea. We may pause it to see if you feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I hate that medicine. It makes me feel awful. If stopping it helps, I’m okay with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll stop it for now. We also noticed your white blood cell count is high. We’re checking for infection but your blood cultures came back clean.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have these painful skin wounds—could they be infected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We cultured one of your thigh wounds. It grew some bacteria, including Pseudomonas, but you don’t have fever or spreading redness, so we think it’s just colonizing the wound, not causing infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. We’ll keep monitoring. We also did an ultrasound of your left breast because we were worried about an abscess, but it looked clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to hear. My skin pain is so bad though—I can’t sleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve asked the palliative care team to help. They’ll adjust your pain meds. We may switch you to oral Dilaudid crushed in ice cream, since you can’t swallow pills right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Ice cream sounds nice. I can usually keep that down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs show your acid levels were off—metabolic acidosis. It’s improving now that we stopped sodium thiosulfate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why I felt so weak?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. The medication was likely the cause. We’ll recheck your labs tomorrow. You’re scheduled for dialysis today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I hope I don’t get sick again after it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your nausea has improved, and you’re eating a bit more. That’s great. We’re switching your anti-nausea med from IV to as-needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, since we stopped that thiosulfate, I feel much better. Can I keep taking my other pills crushed in ice cream?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll continue that. The team will work with outpatient care to make sure they know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count is coming down—now 10.8, which is normal. No signs of infection. Blood and urine cultures were negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We are too. Your GI bleed hasn’t recurred, and your hemoglobin is stable. The GI team still doesn’t recommend an endoscopy since you’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got your wound culture results. Pseudomonas was sensitive to several antibiotics, but since you’re not infected, we won’t treat it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s just living there?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It’s common in chronic wounds. We’ll keep the area clean and monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pain team increased your Dilaudid for breakthrough pain and started a fentanyl patch for constant pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The patch helps. I still need the liquid medicine before dressing changes though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll keep 8mg of Dilaudid scheduled before each dressing change. You’re doing well with pain control now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had some loose stools yesterday. We tested for C. diff—it was negative. Your diarrhea has resolved, so we don’t think it’s serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I think it was from the antibiotics I was on earlier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possible. We’ve stopped unnecessary antibiotics. Your other labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We had a goals of care discussion with your sister. You confirmed you want to keep doing dialysis and focus on quality of life.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’m not ready to stop. I still enjoy things, even with the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We respect that. We’ll support you in continuing dialysis and managing symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your nausea is much better. You’re eating well. We’re confident we can discharge you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Where will I go?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: To an extended care facility. You’ll continue dialysis there and get help with wound care and meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning your discharge meds. You’ll go home with the fentanyl patch, Dilaudid for pain, and we’ll restart sodium thiosulfate at a lower dose if tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can we wait on that? I don’t want to get nauseous again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’ll monitor you as an outpatient. If you tolerate it, we’ll increase slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning are good. White count normal, no acidosis, stable kidneys. You’re ready for discharge planning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I just want to get comfortable somewhere.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The extended care facility confirmed your transfer. They’ll continue your dialysis and help with meds and pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will they crush my pills in ice cream like here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll make sure they know that works best for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re finalizing your discharge. You’ll take Dilaudid for breakthrough pain and before dressing changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the patch?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, fentanyl patch every 72 hours. We’ll review all meds with you before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Last night’s labs are perfect. No anemia, no infection, no acidosis. You’re ready to go tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. Thank you for helping me feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll make sure your sister gets a copy of your care plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today’s the day. You’re being discharged to the extended care facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous but ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed your meds: fentanyl patch, Dilaudid for pain, and your other usual medications. Crush them in ice cream if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And call if I gain more than 3 pounds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And if you have nausea, pain that’s not controlled, or any bleeding, call your doctor right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll follow up with your team at the facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Ms. ___. I’m Dr. ___. You’re in the hospital because you had a seizure during dialysis and also vomited something that looked like coffee grounds. Do you remember what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember being at dialysis… I felt really tired and sick. Then everything went black. My arms were shaking, right? I don’t remember much after that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your arms were jerking, and you were unresponsive for a short time. The team called a code blue. You came out of it after a couple of minutes, but you were confused for a while. We’re concerned this was a seizure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A seizure? But I’ve never had one before! Could it be from the dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re looking into that. You did have coffee-ground emesis—vomiting that looks like old blood—which can happen with stomach irritation. But the seizure is new. We’ve started you on a monitor to check your brain activity.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Brain monitor? Like an EEG?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re doing continuous EEG monitoring because sometimes seizures don’t cause visible shaking—they can just affect awareness. That’s called nonconvulsive status, and we need to rule that out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… that sounds scary. Is that what I had?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The EEG showed abnormal electrical activity in your brain, especially on the right side. It suggests you were in a type of seizure state even after the jerking stopped. We’ve started you on medication called levetiracetam to prevent more seizures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I have to take that forever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll discuss that with the neurology team. For now, it’s important to stay on it. We also ordered a CT scan of your head to check for any bleeding or stroke.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had strokes before… from my heart condition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your history shows a prior stroke with left-sided weakness. We’ll keep that in mind. The CT scan didn’t show any new bleeding, which is good. But we may need an MRI for more detail.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… and what about the vomiting? I’ve been getting nauseous during dialysis a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re treating that with an IV medication called pantoprazole to reduce stomach acid. Since you haven’t vomited again and your blood counts are stable, we don’t think you’re actively bleeding. But we’ll follow up with GI after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. My stomach’s been better since they stopped sodium thiosulfate last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve kept that stopped because it can cause nausea. We’re focusing on managing your calciphylaxis wounds with pain control and dressing changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The ulcers are so painful… especially when they change the dressings.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
